guide.buying.step1.desc: This is sent by the seller’s conveyancer. It will include lots of documents relating to the property. Your conveyancer will review this and raise any legal enquiries they think are necessary.
guide.buying.step1.title: Draft Contract Pack
guide.buying.step2.desc: Your conveyancer will order your searches and review the results of these when they are received. They will also report to you on the terms of mortgage offer.
guide.buying.step2.title: Searches and Mortgage
guide.buying.step3.desc: Your conveyancer will collate all of the property information and legal findings into a property report, which you will read and discuss with them to ensure you are happy.
guide.buying.step3.title: Report
guide.buying.step4.desc: At this point, you can exchange! A completion date will be set in stone, which will be the day that you can collect the keys!
guide.buying.step4.title: Exchange and Completion
guide.buying.step5.desc: Once accepted, you will need to instruct your conveyancer and fill in the onboarding documents, such as client questionnaire and an ID check. You will also need to show your source of funds.
guide.buying.step5.title: Offer Accepted

guide.faq.a1: Usually, your deposit comes from the sale of your current property. If your sale and purchase are linked, the deposit is often transferred up the chain.
guide.faq.a10: This is a legal requirement to prevent fraud and money laundering. Your conveyancer needs to understand where your money is coming from before the transaction can proceed.
guide.faq.a11: You can renegotiate the price, ask the seller to fix issues, or choose not to proceed.
guide.faq.a12: There are additional checks involved, including service charges and management information.
guide.faq.a2: Unfortunately, until exchange, either party can withdraw. You would need to find a new buyer/a new property to purchase and start the process again.
guide.faq.a3: Yes, but it’s less common and can be more stressful. Most transactions have a gap between exchange and completion.
guide.faq.a4: This can often be negotiated, especially if you're in a chain. Your conveyancer will advise based on your situation.
guide.faq.a5: No - you are free to choose your own conveyancer.
guide.faq.a6: Costs can include legal fees, searches, survey fees, mortgage fees, and stamp duty (if applicable).
guide.faq.a7: Most transactions take around 8–12 weeks, but this can vary depending on the chain and how quickly things progress.
guide.faq.a8: Your conveyancer handles all the legal work, carries out checks, liaises with other parties, and guides you through the process from start to finish.
guide.faq.a9: Yes - there are usually initial costs such as searches or money on account before the transaction progresses.
guide.faq.desc: If you’re wondering how any of this works - you are not alone. Here are the questions I get asked most!

guide.faq.q3: Can I exchange and complete on the same day?
guide.faq.q4: What if I don’t have a full 10% deposit?

guide.faq.q6: What costs should I expect when buying?
guide.faq.q7: How long does the process usually take?
guide.faq.q8: What does my conveyancer actually do?
guide.faq.q9: Do I need to pay anything upfront?

guide.selling.step1.desc: Your conveyancer will send this to the buyers. You will need to complete some property questionnaires and provide any documents you have.

guide.selling.step3.desc: If you have a mortgage on the property, your conveyancer will need to order a redemption figure from the Lender. They will also need confirmation of estate agent fees and any other payments due out.

guide.terminology.desc: A quick guide to the legal terms you’ll hear during the process
guide.terminology.t1.def: When transaction becomes legally binding and a completion date is set.
guide.terminology.t10.def: The Lender’s formal confirmation they will lend you the money.
guide.terminology.t11.def: The legal documents sent by the seller’s solicitor to start the transaction.
guide.terminology.t12.def: Documents proving ownership of the property.
guide.terminology.t13.def: A policy used to protect against certain legal risks when they cannot be resolved.
guide.terminology.t14.def: A tax paid (if applicable) when purchasing property.
guide.terminology.t15.def: A percentage of the purchase price paid at exchange.
guide.terminology.t2.def: The day ownership transfers and the buyer receives the keys.
guide.terminology.t3.def: A series of linked buyers and sellers - delays can happen if one part is held up.
guide.terminology.t4.def: Checks carried out with local authorities about the property (eg: planning, roads, environmental issues)
guide.terminology.t5.def: A report that checks the condition of the property
guide.terminology.t6.def: Questions raised about the property by the buyer’s conveyancer.
guide.terminology.t7.def: You own the property and the land it stands on.
guide.terminology.t8.def: You own the property for a fixed period, but not the land it sits on.
guide.terminology.t9.def: A company responsible for maintaining shared areas and collecting service charges.
guide.terminology.title: Terminology Explained
